dataset_metadata.disclaimer: New AI-generated English drafts of the recorded Classical Chinese; not scholarly reviewed. Original source interpretations are not verified geometry or modern etymology.

shuowen:701.text: The sun is about to darken. Formed from 日 amid 茻.

shuowen:702.text: In Nanchang, a dog adept at chasing rabbits in grass is called 莽. Formed from 犬 and 茻; 茻 also indicates the sound.

shuowen:703.text: To conceal. Formed from 死 amid 茻; the 一 within is what provides bedding. The Changes says: “In ancient burials, they wrapped the dead thickly in firewood.”

shuowen:704.text: The minuteness of things. Formed from 八, with 丨 appearing and dividing it. All characters in the 小 category are formed from 小.

shuowen:705.text: Not many. Formed from 小, with 丿 indicating the sound.

shuowen:706.text: Few. Formed from 小, with 乀 indicating the sound. Read like 輟.

shuowen:707.text: To separate. It depicts separation, with the parts facing away from each other. All characters in the 八 category are formed from 八.

shuowen:708.text: To separate. Formed from 八 and 刀: a knife separates things.

shuowen:709.text: A particle expressing certainty. Formed from 入, 丨 and 八; 八 depicts the dispersal of vapor.

shuowen:710.text: A particle drawing out speech. Formed from 八 and 曰, with 𡆧 indicating the sound.

shuowen:711.text: To add further; nearly or hopefully. Formed from 八, with 向 indicating the sound.

shuowen:712.text: To follow one's intention. Formed from 八, with 豕 indicating the sound.

shuowen:713.text: Much speech. Formed from 言, 八 and 厃.

shuowen:714.text: A dividing line. Formed from 八 and 人. Each person has a boundary.

shuowen:715.text: To divide. Formed from repeated 八. 八 means to separate and also indicates the sound. The Explanation of the Classic of Filial Piety says: “Thus superior and inferior have their distinctions.”

shuowen:716.text: To divide equally. Formed from 八 and 厶 (pronounced 司). 八 suggests turning one's back. Han Fei said: “Turning one's back on 厶, private interest, makes 公, public fairness.”

shuowen:717.text: A dividing standard or boundary marker. Formed from 八 and 弋, with 弋 also indicating the sound; by extension, “necessary” or “certain.”

shuowen:718.text: An extended utterance. Formed from 八, with abbreviated 舍 indicating the sound.

shuowen:719.text: To distinguish. It depicts the separated toes and claws of a beast. All characters in the 釆 category are formed from 釆. Read like 辨.

shuowen:720.text: A beast's foot is called 番. Formed from 釆; 田 depicts its sole.

shuowen:721.text: To know fully; to understand with careful discernment. Formed from 宀 and 釆. Xu Kai says: “宀 means to cover; 釆, to distinguish. Encompassing something and distinguishing it deeply: 宷 means fully.”

shuowen:722.text: Thorough and exhaustive. Formed from 心 and 釆.

shuowen:723.text: To untie or explain. Formed from 釆, taking its sense of distinguishing things, with 睪 indicating the sound.

shuowen:724.text: To divide a thing through the middle. Formed from 八 and 牛: cattle are large things that can be divided. All characters in the 半 category are formed from 半.

shuowen:725.text: Meat from half a body. Another explanation: broad flesh. Formed from 半 and 肉; 半 also indicates the sound.

shuowen:726.text: To split in half. Formed from 半, with 反 indicating the sound.

shuowen:727.text: Cattle, a major animal for sacrifice and agricultural work. The text offers an early interpretive association with 件, or the ordering of affairs, and describes a form depicting horns, head and body. All characters in the 牛 category are formed from 牛. [Duan argues that some transmitted explanatory wording is a later interpolation.]

shuowen:728.text: The male parent among livestock. Formed from 牛, with 土 indicating the sound.

shuowen:729.text: A bull. Formed from 牛, with 岡 indicating the sound.

shuowen:730.text: 朴特, the male parent of cattle. Formed from 牛, with 寺 indicating the sound.

shuowen:731.text: The female parent among livestock. Formed from 牛, with 匕 indicating the sound. The Changes says: “Rearing a cow is auspicious.”

shuowen:732.text: A calf. Formed from 牛, with abbreviated 瀆 indicating the sound.

shuowen:733.text: A two-year-old ox. Formed from 牛, with 巿 indicating the sound.

shuowen:734.text: A three-year-old ox. Formed from 牛, with 參 indicating the sound.

shuowen:735.text: A four-year-old ox. Formed from 牛 and 四; 四 also indicates the sound.

shuowen:736.text: A castrated ox. Formed from 牛, with 害 indicating the sound.

shuowen:737.text: An ox with mingled white and black hair. Formed from 牛, with 尨 indicating the sound.

shuowen:738.text: A mottled ox, 牻牛. Formed from 牛, with 京 indicating the sound. The Spring and Autumn commentary says: “牻㹁.”

shuowen:739.text: An ox with a white backbone. Formed from 牛, with 厲 indicating the sound.

shuowen:740.text: A yellow ox with tiger markings. Formed from 牛, with 余 indicating the sound. Read like 塗.

shuowen:741.text: A mottled ox. Formed from 牛, with abbreviated 勞 indicating the sound.

shuowen:742.text: An ox with a white backbone. Formed from 牛, with 寽 indicating the sound.

shuowen:743.text: An ox with star-like patches. Formed from 牛, with 平 indicating the sound.

shuowen:744.text: An ox of yellowish-white color. Formed from 牛, with 麃 indicating the sound.

shuowen:745.text: A yellow ox with black lips. Formed from 牛, with 𦎫 indicating the sound. The Odes says: “Ninety are his black-lipped oxen.”

shuowen:746.text: A white ox. Formed from 牛, with 隺 indicating the sound.

shuowen:747.text: An ox with a long backbone. Formed from 牛, with 畺 indicating the sound.

shuowen:748.text: An ox walking slowly. Formed from 牛, with 𠬢 indicating the sound. Read like 滔.

shuowen:749.text: The sound of an ox breathing. Formed from 牛, with 雔 indicating the sound. Another explanation: the name of an ox.

shuowen:750.text: The lowing of cattle. Formed from 牛, depicting its vocal breath issuing from its mouth.

shuowen:751.text: Livestock of unblemished, uniform appearance. Formed from 牛, with 産 indicating the sound.

shuowen:752.text: An ox complete and unblemished. Formed from 牛, with 生 indicating the sound.

shuowen:753.text: An ox of uniform color. Formed from 牛, with 全 indicating the sound.

shuowen:754.text: To lead forward. Formed from 牛, depicting the cord leading an ox. 玄 indicates the sound.

shuowen:755.text: A cattle-and-horse pen. Formed from 牛, with 告 indicating the sound. The Book of Zhou says: “Now pen the cattle and horses.”

shuowen:756.text: An enclosure for rearing cattle and horses. Formed from 牛 and abbreviated 冬, taking its sense of surrounding on all four sides.

shuowen:757.text: To rear cattle on fodder stalks. Formed from 牛 and 芻; 芻 also indicates the sound. The Spring and Autumn Discourses of the States says: “How many fodder-fed and grain-fed animals?”

shuowen:758.text: An ox gentle and tractable. Formed from 牛, with 夒 indicating the sound.

shuowen:759.text: The Changes says: “Yoke cattle and ride horses.” Formed from 牛, with 𤰈 indicating the sound.

shuowen:760.text: To plow. Formed from 牛, with 黎 indicating the sound.

shuowen:761.text: Two oxen plowing inward from opposite sides of a field. Formed from 牛, with 非 indicating the sound. Another explanation: to plow a field again and sow it. Pronounced like 匪.

shuowen:762.text: Cattle or sheep without offspring. Formed from 牛, with 𠷎 indicating the sound. Read like 糗 in 糗糧, dry provisions.

shuowen:763.text: To butt. Formed from 牛, with 氐 indicating the sound.

shuowen:764.text: An ox kicking and butting, 踶𤜂. Formed from 牛, with 衞 indicating the sound.

shuowen:765.text: An obstinate ox that refuses to be led. Formed from 牛 and 臤; 臤 also indicates the sound. Another explanation: a large appearance. Read like 賢.

shuowen:766.text: The bone below an ox's knee. Formed from 牛, with 巠 indicating the sound. The Spring and Autumn commentary says: “Sima Keng of Song had the courtesy name Niu.”

shuowen:767.text: A disease of an ox's tongue. Formed from 牛, with 今 indicating the sound.

shuowen:768.text: A bovine beyond the southern frontier, resembling a pig, with one horn on its nose and one on its crown. Formed from 牛, with 㞑 indicating the sound.

shuowen:769.text: 牣 means full. Formed from 牛, with 刃 indicating the sound. The Odes says: “Ah, full of leaping fish!”

shuowen:770.text: The myriad things. Cattle are great things; the reckoning of heaven and earth begins at the Ox-Leader asterism, hence formed from 牛. 勿 indicates the sound.

shuowen:771.text: A sacrificial animal for the ancestral temple. Formed from 牛, with 羲 indicating the sound. Palace Attendant Jia explains: this is not an ancient character.

shuowen:772.text: A castrated ox. Formed from 牛, with 建 indicating the sound. Also the name of a commandery.

shuowen:773.text: An ox without horns. Formed from 牛, with 童 indicating the sound. Ancient usage also writes 僮.

shuowen:774.text: The long-haired ox of the southwestern Yi peoples. Formed from 牛, with 𠩺 indicating the sound. All characters in the 犛 category are formed from 犛.

shuowen:775.text: A yak's tail. Formed from abbreviated 犛 and 毛.

shuowen:776.text: Stiff, curled hair usable as padding to raise clothing. Formed from abbreviated 犛, with 來 indicating the sound.

shuowen:777.text: When an ox butts people, a crosspiece is attached to its horns to warn them. Formed from 口 and 牛. The Changes says: “The young ox's horn restraint.” All characters in the 告 category are formed from 告.

shuowen:778.text: An especially urgent announcement. Formed from 告, with abbreviated 學 indicating the sound.

shuowen:779.text: That by which people speak and eat. A pictograph. All characters in the 口 category are formed from 口.

shuowen:780.text: To roar. Formed from 口, with 敫 indicating the sound. Another explanation: 噭 means to call out.

shuowen:781.text: A beak. Formed from 口, with 蜀 indicating the sound.

shuowen:782.text: A mouth. Formed from 口, with 彖 indicating the sound.

shuowen:783.text: The edge of the mouth. Formed from 口, with 勿 indicating the sound.

shuowen:784.text: The throat. Formed from 口, with 龍 indicating the sound.

shuowen:785.text: The throat, 咽. Formed from 口, with 侯 indicating the sound.

shuowen:786.text: The throat, where breath and voice converge. Formed from 口, with 會 indicating the sound. Read like 快. Another explanation relates it to voracious or greedy eating. [The transmitted wording of the alternative gloss differs between editions.]

shuowen:787.text: To swallow. Formed from 口, with 天 indicating the sound.

shuowen:788.text: The throat, 嗌. Formed from 口, with 因 indicating the sound.

shuowen:789.text: The throat, 咽. Formed from 口, with 益 indicating the sound.

shuowen:790.text: A large mouth. Formed from 口, with 軍 indicating the sound.

shuowen:791.text: To open the mouth. Formed from 口, with 多 indicating the sound.

shuowen:792.text: The sound of an infant crying. Formed from 口, with 瓜 indicating the sound. The Odes says: “Hou Ji cried.”

shuowen:793.text: An infant's sound. Formed from 口, with 秋 indicating the sound.

shuowen:794.text: An infant's sound. Formed from 口, with 皇 indicating the sound. The Odes says: “Its crying was loud.”

shuowen:795.text: In Chaoxian, an infant's unceasing crying is called 咺. Formed from 口, with abbreviated 宣 indicating the sound.

shuowen:796.text: In Qin and Jin, an infant's unceasing crying is called 唴. Formed from 口, with 羌 indicating the sound.

shuowen:797.text: In Chu, an infant's unceasing crying is called 噭咷. Formed from 口, with 兆 indicating the sound.

shuowen:798.text: In Song and Qi, an infant's unceasing crying is called 喑. Formed from 口, with 音 indicating the sound.

shuowen:799.text: An infant showing understanding. Formed from 口, with 疑 indicating the sound. The Odes says: “Able to be discerning and understanding.”

shuowen:800.text: An infant laughing. Formed from 口, with 亥 indicating the sound.
